To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the net GHG footprint of biofuel production is strongly influenced by agronomic practices, 2) perennial grasses have the potential to increase soil C stock, 3) perennial grasses can reduce GHG footprint by reducing the need for fertilizer, 4) the net GHGP of napiergrass is comparable to sugarcane in the first two years, and 5) napiergrass is more resilient to drought than sugarcane.
the net GHG balance of perennial tropical grass biofuels is not negative, but can be positive or negative depending upon the crop choice and management.

the perennial grasses we evaluated have the potential to reduce net GHG production in tropical bioenergy systems, but that the magnitude of the effect depends on the crop choice and water and nutrient management practices.

the potential for bioenergy feedstocks to mitigate climate change by sequestering soil C and replacing fossil fuels with perennial grasses.

developing a more comprehensive approach to evaluating the environmental sustainability of bioenergy systems, and we show how a field-based approach that includes soil carbon stock, crop yield, and net GHG flux can be used to evaluate the potential of a bioenergy system for mitigating greenhouse warming.

the environmental impacts of replacing annual arables with perennial bioenergy grasses in tropical, humid climates and suggests that the choice of perennial biofuel feedstocks and deficit irrigation management can be used to reduce GHG emissions and increase soil C sequestration in the tropics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
napiergrass has the potential to replace sugarcane as the dominant biofuel feedstock on Oahu.
the GHG balance of perennial tropical biofuels is positive, but that the magnitude depends on agronomic management and the choice of perennial crop.
the net GWP of perennial grasses for biofuel in Hawaii is not higher than sugarcane.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
perennial, ratoon-harved napiergrass has a net GWP that is similar to or less than that of conventional sugarcane, depending upon the level of irrigation deficit and the frequency of ratoon harvests.

perennial biofuel feedstocks, with appropriate agronomic practices, have the potential to reduce GHG emissions and increase soil C stock, and that perennial feedstocks can have a lower GWP compared to annual crops.
the choice of biofuel feedstock and water management are critical to reducing GHG emissions from biofuel production systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
perennial biofuel feedstocks have the capacity to sequester soil C and mitigate GHG emissions.
the GWP of perennial tropical biofuel feedstocks is highly sensitive to agronomic management, and that the choice of feedstock can be critical to the net GWP of bioenergy systems.
perennial biofuels, if grown on marginal land, can reduce net GHG emissions, even if grown in tropical regions where the climate change mitigation benefits are often assumed to be minimal.
